flagged.evidence: It says, “Equivalently, A=(LD)U is a normalised LU factorisation.” But def-normalised-lu-factorisation defines normalised LU by requiring its left factor to have every diagonal entry equal to 1. In an LDU factorisation diag(LD)=diag(D), which need not be 1; the scoped example uses D=diag(2,3). The normalised LU regrouping is A=L(DU), not (LD)U.

The step concludes, “By [L1], this updated matrix is exactly the start of the upper-triangular factor.” The cited theorem requires unpivoted elimination to reach an upper-triangular matrix “without encountering a zero pivot.” The example's displayed post-first-step matrix has its next pivot a_22=0, so that hypothesis fails and it does not produce the cited normalised LU upper factor.

The theorem covers F=R or C. Its floating-point dependency defines a floating-point system as a set F contained in R, and its cited dot-product theorem assumes x,y in R^n. No componentwise complex floating-point model or complex dot-product error theorem is assumed, so the cited facts do not license the asserted complex case.

Step 1.1 gives P-hat A+E=L-hat U-hat, then step 2.1 sets Delta A=P-hat^T E and claims that “|Delta A_ij| has the same bound as |E_ij| entrywise.” A nontrivial permutation instead gives |Delta A_ij|=|E_{pi(i),j}|. Thus the entrywise bound must have its row factor permuted, namely |Delta A| <= gamma_n P-hat^T(|L-hat||U-hat|), not the Statement's unpermuted row-i bound.

The statement includes complex matrices. However, def-standard-relative-floating-point-model-and-unit-roundoff defines rounding only for a finite set contained in R, and thm-floating-point-dot-product-componentwise-and-normwise-error-bounds is explicitly for real vectors. No complex floating-point arithmetic assumption is supplied for the claimed complex QR result.

Step 1.1 has A^(k+1)=H-hat_k(A^(k)+E_k), so after the first step A^(1) already includes the nonzero local rounding perturbation E_0. Step 3.1 nevertheless says every A^(k) is obtained from a trailing block of A only by unitary transformations and deletions, and concludes ||A^(k)||_F <= ||A||_F. That does not follow in the floating-point model: prior E_j terms remain in the active block. This unsupported bound is essential to the displayed 3n gamma_m estimate.

The theorem quantifies over an arbitrary field F, but its proof chooses a pivot with “|a| maximal” and cites def-permutation-matrix-partial-pivoting-and-pivot-growth. That definition begins “Let F=R or C” and defines partial pivoting through entry modulus. Partial pivoting by maximal modulus is not defined for a general field, so the stated field domain is too broad.

The Statement leaves the field F unrestricted while requiring greedy maximal residual 2-norm pivoting. Its cited computational-QR definition explicitly assumes F=R or C. A residual 2-norm and its maximisation are not supplied for an arbitrary field, so the theorem needs that field hypothesis.

This item applies to F=R or C and uses A* A. But [L4] cites thm-normal-equations-square-the-spectral-condition-number, whose Statement assumes A in M_{m×n}(R) and proves the result for A^T A. That dependency does not support the complex claim as cited.

It asserts 2 sum_{k=0}^{n-1}(m-k)(n-k)=2mn^2-(2/3)n^3+O(mn). At m=n, the left side is 2 sum_{h=1}^n h^2=(2/3)n^3+O(n^2), while the asserted right side is (4/3)n^3+O(n^2). The displayed summation does not yield the stated Householder count.

It asserts 3 sum_{k=0}^{n-1}(m-k-1)(n-k)=3mn^2-n^3+O(mn). At m=n, the left side is 3 sum_{h=1}^n(h-1)h=n^3-n, whereas the asserted right side is 2n^3+O(n^2). The Givens summation therefore cannot establish the stated operation count.
